\chapter{Before and After}
\label{ch:ml-before-after}
\hlchaptermodality{106}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that something happens before or after a named time or a named event.}

From cold: the two words that order events, and the ending they both lean on.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[munpŭ]{\ml{മുൻപ്} — before}

\label{lesson:ML-C106-munpu}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{at two o'clock}. Then say the word you have for \textbf{then} — the one that puts one turn after another.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{മുൻപ്}} (\emph{munpŭ}) — \textbf{before}.

\textbf{It goes after.} English puts \emph{before} in front of what it is before; Malayalam puts it behind:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്} \ml{മുൻപ്}} — \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ munpŭ} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{before} two o'clock.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Read the two \textbf{phrases} right to left and they come out as English: \emph{before} — \emph{two o'clock}. Keep \textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണി}} together as one piece.

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Look at what it is standing on.} \textbf{\ml{മണിക്ക്}} — the hour with the dative on it, exactly as you built it. \textbf{\ml{മുൻപ്}} does not attach to the word and does not change it. It is a separate word that leans on an ending you already make.

The word itself is built on \textbf{mun}, the old Dravidian word for the \textbf{front}. What is in front of you in space became what is in front of you in time.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{munpŭ}
  \item \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ munpŭ}
  \item which word carries the ending, and which one leans on it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{Before two o'clock}? (\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്} \ml{മുൻപ്}}.) Where does \textbf{\ml{മുൻപ്}} stand — in front of the hour or after it? (\textbf{After it}.) What is it built on? (\textbf{mun}, the word for the \textbf{front}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[śēṣaṁ]{\ml{ശേഷം} — after}

\label{lesson:ML-C106-shesham}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{before two o'clock}. Then say the word for the meal.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{ശേഷം}} (\emph{śēṣaṁ}) — \textbf{after}.

It stands where \textbf{\ml{മുൻപ്}} stands, on the same kind of ending:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഊണിന്} \ml{ശേഷം}} — \emph{ūṇinŭ śēṣaṁ} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{after} the meal.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same case, wearing its other shape}]
\textbf{\ml{ഊണിന്}} is the dative again — and it is the \textbf{other} of the two shapes you were given. You were told the choice is made by the sound the word finishes on, and here is the part of that you can use: a word ending in a \textbf{consonant} takes \textbf{-\ml{ിന്}}. \textbf{\ml{ഊണ്}} ends in \textbf{\ml{ണ്}}, so \textbf{-\ml{ിന്}} it is. The hour ended in a vowel and took \textbf{-\ml{ക്ക്}}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്} \ml{മുൻപ്}} & \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ munpŭ} & before two o'clock \\
\textbf{\ml{ഊണിന്} \ml{ശേഷം}} & \emph{ūṇinŭ śēṣaṁ} & after the meal \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Same case, two shapes, and both of these words lean on it.} You are not learning a new piece of machinery — you are hanging two more words on a piece you have had since your first case ending.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{\ml{ശേഷം}} is Sanskrit, and its plain meaning is \textbf{the remainder} — what is left over. \emph{After the meal} is, in the word's own terms, \textbf{what is left of the day once the meal is done}.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{śēṣaṁ}
  \item \emph{ūṇinŭ śēṣaṁ}
  \item \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ munpŭ}, then \emph{ūṇinŭ śēṣaṁ} — and name the two shapes of the one ending
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{After the meal}? (\textbf{\ml{ഊണിന്} \ml{ശേഷം}}.) Which two shapes of the dative did this chapter use? (\textbf{-\ml{ക്ക്}} on the hour, \textbf{-\ml{ിന്}} on the meal.) What does \textbf{\ml{ശേഷം}} plainly mean? (\textbf{The remainder} — what is left over.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{\ml{ആദ്യം}, \ml{പിന്നെ}, \ml{മുൻപ്}, \ml{ശേഷം} — ordering a run, and ordering against a point}

\label{lesson:ML-C106-ordering}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{at first}. Say \emph{then}. You have had both for a long while.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
You now have four words about order, and they split into \textbf{two pairs that do different jobs} — though not the job you might expect.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ആദ്യം}}, \textbf{\ml{പിന്നെ}} & \emph{ādyaṁ}, \emph{pinne} & order a \textbf{run} of things \\
\textbf{\ml{മുൻപ്}}, \textbf{\ml{ശേഷം}} & \emph{munpŭ}, \emph{śēṣaṁ} & order one thing against a \textbf{named point} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Both pairs order real events.} You were shown \textbf{\ml{ആദ്യം} \ml{ഊണ്}, \ml{പിന്നെ} \ml{ചായ}} — lunch first, then tea — and that is the world being ordered, not a story about it.

\textbf{What the first pair cannot do is name what it is measuring against.} It lays things out in a run: this, then that. \textbf{\ml{മുൻപ്}} and \textbf{\ml{ശേഷം}} do something the other pair has no way to do — they take a \textbf{named} time or event and place something relative to it.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ādyaṁ}, then \emph{pinne} — laying a run out in order
  \item \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ munpŭ} — ordering an event against an hour
  \item \emph{ūṇinŭ śēṣaṁ} — ordering an event against a meal
  \item which two of the four need a named thing to measure against
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{Until this chapter you could put events in a run and not anchor them.} \emph{First lunch, then tea} says which came first and says nothing about when either happened. \emph{Before two o'clock} and \emph{after the meal} fix an event against a point you have \textbf{named}.

That is the whole of what the two new words add — and neither of them needed a new piece of grammar to do it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two lay a run out in order? (\textbf{\ml{ആദ്യം}} and \textbf{\ml{പിന്നെ}}.) Which two measure against a named point? (\textbf{\ml{മുൻപ്}} and \textbf{\ml{ശേഷം}}.) In this chapter, what did that named thing wear? (\textbf{The dative}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[munpuṁ śēṣavuṁ enna ōrmma]{(before, after) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R106-before-after-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{before} and \emph{after}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: both of them lean, and neither of them attaches}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്} \ml{മുൻപ്}} & \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ munpŭ} & before two o'clock \\
\textbf{\ml{ഊണിന്} \ml{ശേഷം}} & \emph{ūṇinŭ śēṣaṁ} & after the meal \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Neither word joined onto the word in front of it.} They stay separate words — but they are not passengers: it is \textbf{\ml{ശേഷം}} that puts \textbf{\ml{ഊണ്}} into the dative in the first place. The hour was already going to wear that ending; the meal wears it because the postposition asks for it.

Both stand \textbf{behind} what they are about, which is the opposite of where English puts them.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{The ending underneath both of them is your first case ending}, and it has been busy. It was glossed \emph{to} and \emph{for}. It carries the person who knows, wants or has something — \textbf{\ml{എനിക്ക്}}. You put it on an hour to mean \emph{at}. And now these two postpositions lean on it as well. No new machinery in this chapter at all.

And you can now order in two ways: \textbf{\ml{ആദ്യം}} and \textbf{\ml{പിന്നെ}} lay a run out, while \textbf{\ml{മുൻപ്}} and \textbf{\ml{ശേഷം}} measure against a point you name.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{munpŭ}, then \emph{śēṣaṁ}
  \item \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ munpŭ}
  \item \emph{ūṇinŭ śēṣaṁ}
  \item where these two stand, compared with where English puts them
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{Before two o'clock}? (\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്} \ml{മുൻപ്}}.) \emph{After the meal}? (\textbf{\ml{ഊണിന്} \ml{ശേഷം}}.) Do they go in front of the thing or behind it? (\textbf{Behind}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
